# Does the model travel? A comparative benchmark across climates, demographics and countries

**Status:** methodology and data provenance are final; the results tables are generated by
`eval/comparative_report.py` into `results/comparative.md` and are reproduced there rather
than copied here.

---

## 1. Why this study exists

Every number this repository has published comes from four buildings at one site
in Tempe, Arizona. `data/buildings.json` has always said so in plain terms:

> "It is not India, and the load shapes are American."

That is an honest disclosure and it is also a standing objection. A reviewer is
entitled to ask whether the method is general or whether it is a careful fit to
Phoenix, and the question is not answered by asserting generality. It is
answered by running the identical pipeline elsewhere and reporting what happens,
including — especially — where it stops working.

This study does that along three axes, and adds real Indian data, which the
project has never had.

---

## 2. Design

Three arms. Each holds everything fixed except one factor, which is the same
discipline the repository's ablation already uses on the forecaster.

| Arm | Held fixed | Varied | Answers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Climate** | demographic (Education) | site, country | is the method climate-general? |
| **Office** | demographic (Office) | site, country | is the climate finding an artefact of one usage class? |
| **Demographic** | climate (Washington DC) | usage class | does it hold across building types? |
| **National** | — | country | does the forecaster work on real Indian demand? |

Education is the control for the climate arm because it is the only usage class
that survives the selection rule at every site on the ladder. Office is run as a
narrower second ladder precisely so that a climate result cannot be dismissed as
something peculiar to schools.

### Selection is by rule, never by hand

Buildings are chosen by the *identical* rule already stated in
`data/buildings.json`, applied by `data/sites.py` to all nineteen BDG2 sites:

- no district chilled-water meter, so the electricity meter actually contains
  the cooling we intend to control
- coverage above 97% in the split window
- median load between 40 and 800 kW
- positive load-versus-outdoor-temperature correlation

Inside a `(site, usage)` cell the tie-break is the repository's own stated
criterion for why `Fox_office_Gaylord` is the primary building: the sharpest
demand-charge exposure, `p99/median`.

That the uniform rule re-selects `Fox_office_Gaylord` — the building originally
picked by hand — is a small but real check that the rule encodes the judgement
it was meant to.

### The protocol is unchanged

Same 15-month train / 2-month validate / 1-month test split, same temporal
ordering, same conformal calibration, same five models. Nothing about the method
was tuned per site. A site that does badly is reported doing badly.

---

## 3. What the selection rule discovers about itself

Applying the rule across all nineteen sites produces a result before a single
model is trained, and it is worth stating on its own.

**251 buildings across 11 sites and 3 countries pass.** But the failures are
more informative than the passes:

- **The two hottest sites in BDG2 yield nothing.** Gator and Panther (Orlando,
  cooling-degree-day share 0.90 — the closest climates in the dataset to an
  Indian metro) have no building that passes, because none has adequate coverage
  in the split window. The sites most like the target market are the ones the
  data will not support.
- **The fourth clause is regional, and does not survive travel.** "Positive
  load-versus-temperature correlation" is a sanity check at Fox, where every
  candidate is cooling-dominated. Applied to Minneapolis or Dublin it removes
  most of the site, because those buildings consume electricity when it is
  *cold*. A further **77 buildings across 9 sites** pass every other clause and
  fail only this one. They are not bad buildings; the rule is carrying a Phoenix
  assumption.

Both facts are reported by `data/sites.py` and neither was anticipated when the
rule was written.

---

## 4. Data provenance

Nothing here is vendored; every source is fetched by script.

### Tier 1 — building level

**Building Data Genome Project 2.** 1,578 metered buildings, 19 sites, three
countries. The only harmonised multi-country building dataset that exists, which
is why it carries the controlled comparison: the same physical quantity, the same
metering convention, the same period.

It contains **no Indian buildings**. That is a hard limit of the data, and
relabelling an American building as Indian would be worse than the gap.

### Tier 2 — system level, and where India enters

Because Tier 1 cannot supply India, Tier 2 goes and gets real Indian demand from
a different source. There is no building to control at this level — but the
thing under benchmark is the *model*, and a quantile load forecaster is exactly
as testable on a city's demand as on a building's.

| Series | Source | Native resolution | Window |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **India — Delhi** | Delhi SLDC, via the `Ecohen4/Delhi` archive | **15 min** | 2011–2012, 100% coverage |
| Great Britain | ENTSO-E via Open Power System Data | 60 min | 2016-01 – 2017-06 |
| Ireland | ENTSO-E via OPSD | 60 min | 2016-01 – 2017-06 |
| Germany | ENTSO-E via OPSD | 60 min | 2016-01 – 2017-06 |
| France | ENTSO-E via OPSD | 60 min | 2016-01 – 2017-06 |
| Spain | ENTSO-E via OPSD | 60 min | 2016-01 – 2017-06 |

Weather for every Tier 2 series is ERA5 hourly reanalysis from the Open-Meteo
archive, free and keyless, at the city coordinate.

The Delhi series is 15-minute *natively* — the same resolution the controller
runs at, and the only series in the whole project that does not have to be
upsampled from hourly.

---

## 5. Two defects this study found in our own pipeline

A comparative run is also a test of the code, and it failed twice. Both are
fixed; both were real.

**The feature block was quietly American.** `forecast/features.py` hard-coded
twenty US federal holiday dates. Run on a London building, it would have labelled
the last Monday in May an ordinary working day and the fourth Thursday in
November a holiday — precisely inverted, on two of the largest load anomalies in
the year. Every cross-country number would have carried a defect owing nothing to
the model. Holidays are now a function of country
(`forecast/calendars.py`), and India is the case that proves the point: a large
share of Indian public holidays are lunisolar and move against the Gregorian
calendar, so they cannot be a fixed list at all.

The US 2016–17 set is preserved verbatim as the default, and the change was
verified not to move a single existing number: rebuilding the Fox feature frame
after the patch leaves `is_holiday`, `cdd_fut`, `t_out_fut`, `is_weekend` and
`horizon` all exactly equal, with the only residual a 1.3e-07 rolling-standard-
deviation accumulation artefact, nine orders of magnitude below any reported
quantity.

**`data/prepare.py` clobbered its own manifest.** It writes one manifest per
run, so preparing a second site silently discarded the first. Single-site work
never exposed it. It now merges, and takes a `--manifest` argument so the
comparative panel cannot touch the main one.

---

## 6. Why skill, not pinball loss

Absolute pinball loss is not comparable across these rows and it would be
dishonest to tabulate it as though it were. A 3,000 MW city and a 60 kW building
are different units; Delhi's window (2011–12) does not overlap Europe's
(2016–17).

The headline metric is therefore **skill against each series' own seasonal-naive
baseline**:

```
skill = 1 - pinball(ours) / pinball(seasonal naive)
```

a ratio computed entirely inside one series' own data and its own period, and so
comparable across both. Absolute figures are printed alongside, and nothing is
concluded from them across rows.

Seasonal naive is the right denominator rather than a convenient one. It is what
a site can do on day one with no model at all, and this repository's own ablation
already found it reaching zero ceiling breaches on a calm month. Beating it has
to be earned.

---

## 7. Limitations, written before the results

In keeping with `docs/limitations.md`, these are stated in advance.

1. **Tier 2 is a forecasting benchmark, not a control benchmark.** There is no
   building, no thermal mass and no HVAC to shift at system level. It tests the
   model, which is what was asked. It does not test the controller, and no
   savings claim is made from it.
2. **The Delhi window does not overlap the European one.** Mitigated by
   reporting skill rather than absolute loss, but not eliminated. A 2011 Indian
   grid is not a 2016 European one in any respect.
3. **Capital-city temperature is a proxy for national load-weighted
   temperature.** Defensible for Great Britain and Ireland; rough for Germany,
   France and Spain, which are large and climatically varied. Delhi is a city,
   so the proxy problem does not arise there.
4. **Cold-start transfer is expected to be poor and this study does not fix
   it.** `results/cold_start.md` already shows the model losing to seasonal naive
   on an unseen building *at the same site*. Nothing here should be read as a
   claim that weights transfer across countries. The claim under test is that the
   *architecture and protocol* travel.
5. **The demographic arm is one city.** Holding climate fixed means the
   demographic result is Washington DC's, and a second city would be needed to
   separate demographic from local building stock.
6. **Delhi is one Indian city.** It is real Indian data, which the project did
   not have before. It is not a claim about India.
